planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or set out container plants in fall or spring, in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; this natural hybrid between Cistus ladanifer and Cistus creticus resents rich soil, heavy mulch, and summer irrigation once established.

directions: Set plants in lean, fast-draining, alkaline-to-neutral soil in full sun, spacing them wide enough to allow air movement through the rounded, wiry-stemmed mound. This vigorous hybrid produces a long midsummer show of 3-inch, crinkled, orchid-pink flowers, each petal marked at the base with a deep maroon blotch that forms a dark ring around the yellow-anthered center, and although each bloom lasts only a single day, a well-grown plant carries dozens of buds in constant succession for weeks. The narrow, gray-green, resinous leaves stay evergreen and aromatic through mild winters but the plant is intolerant of wet feet, so avoid low spots or heavy clay. Shear lightly after the main flush to keep growth compact, since old wood does not reliably resprout if cut back hard.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or set out container plants in fall or early spring, in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; the lowest and most spreading of the commonly grown rockroses, useful for banks and dry slopes.

directions: Plant in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun where the wide, low, arching branches can spread unobstructed into a dense mat. Sageleaf rockrose takes its name from its dull, gray-green, wrinkled leaves that resemble common garden sage, and in late spring the plant disappears under a blanket of single white flowers about 1.5 inches across, each marked with a small yellow blotch at the base of the petals. Because it stays under 2 feet tall while spreading 4 feet or more, it is one of the best cistus choices for erosion control on dry banks, for cascading over low walls, or as a rock-garden groundcover, and it tolerates coastal salt spray and poor, rocky soil that would rot most other shrubs. Avoid overhead irrigation and rich soil, both of which shorten its lifespan and promote fungal problems.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or set out container plants in fall or spring, in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; a compact hybrid cultivar selected for its especially vivid flower color and tidy, rounded habit.

directions: Grow in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun, allowing the plant to form its naturally neat, mounded shape without competition from taller neighbors. 'Sunset' is prized for its intensely saturated, hot magenta-pink flowers that read almost fluorescent in bright sun, each bloom carrying a darker central zone that intensifies the color contrast against the small, dark, resinous evergreen leaves. It stays noticeably more compact and rounded than many cistus hybrids, making it well suited to smaller borders, raised beds, or large containers where a more sprawling rockrose would outgrow the space. Like all cistus, it thrives on neglect once established and should never be fertilized or watered as though it were an ordinary garden shrub, since lush growth from rich conditions makes the plant floppy and short-lived.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants after the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; one of the more cold-hardy and vigorous cherry-red selections widely planted along the Gulf Coast.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — keep it away from areas grazed by livestock or pets and never burn the trimmings. Root cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun. 'Calypso' produces single, cherry-red flowers in dense clusters from late spring through fall on a fast-growing, upright shrub, and it has earned a reputation among Gulf Coast growers as one of the hardier red-flowered oleanders, resprouting reliably from the base after the freezes that kill less cold-tolerant reds to the ground. It makes an excellent large screening hedge or background planting where its size and vigor can be put to use, tolerating heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil with equal ease.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants after the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; an especially large, vigorous white-flowered selection long grown throughout the Gulf South.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — site it well away from grazing animals, small children, and open flames, since burning the wood releases toxic smoke. Root cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun. 'Sister Agnes' is one of the most widely planted white oleanders in the South, valued for its unusually vigorous, upright growth to well over 10 feet and its heavy, near-continuous production of large, pure white, single flowers from late spring into fall. Its size and density make it a classic choice for a tall, informal privacy screen or windbreak along property lines and highway margins, and like other oleanders it shrugs off heat, drought, salt spray, and neglect once established, needing only an annual thinning of old canes to stay full from the ground up.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants after the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; a naturally dwarf, compact selection suited to foundation plantings, low hedges, and containers where full-size oleanders are too large.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — keep it out of reach of grazing animals and small children, and never burn the prunings. Root cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun. 'Petite Pink' stays dwarf and dense, typically 4 to 6 feet tall and wide, making it far better suited than standard oleanders to foundation plantings, low informal hedges, median strips, and large patio containers. It carries soft, clear pink single flowers in loose clusters from late spring through fall and requires only light shaping to maintain its naturally rounded form. As with the species, it is exceptionally heat-, drought-, and salt-tolerant, thriving in the same lean, well-drained conditions and reflected heat that would stress most other flowering shrubs.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants after the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; grown primarily for its cream-and-green variegated foliage in addition to its flowers.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — site it away from grazing animals and small children, and never burn the trimmings. Root cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun. Unlike most oleanders grown chiefly for flower color, 'Turner's Carnival' earns its place in the garden for its long, lance-shaped leaves boldly striped in cream and gray-green, giving the whole shrub a lit-up, variegated presence even between bloom cycles; single pink flowers appear in clusters from late spring through fall as a secondary attraction. Some reversion to solid green foliage can occur on older wood, so prune out any all-green shoots promptly to keep the variegation prominent throughout the plant. It shares the species' tolerance for heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil, making it a striking accent for a sunny border where its foliage can be appreciated up close.
